mcqs.q: To a computer, a photo is really a grid of…
mcqs.e: An image is a grid of number-pixels - the start of computer vision.

mcqs.q: A model splits your sentence into sub-word pieces before processing. A practical consequence of working on these pieces (not letters) is that the model…
o: can miscount the letters in a word
reads one character at a time
mcqs.e: Working on tokens (sub-word pieces) explains why a model can miscount letters or mis-split rare words.

mcqs.q: Raising the temperature setting of a generative model usually makes its output…
mcqs.e: Higher temperature increases randomness/creativity; lower temperature makes output more focused and predictable.

mcqs.q: Word embeddings represent words as vectors so that…
o: every single word receives an identical vector
words get directly converted into images
vectors are always limited to two numbers each
words with similar meanings sit close together
mcqs.e: Embeddings place similar meanings near each other, letting models measure how related words are.

mcqs.q: In supervised learning, the training data includes…
mcqs.e: Supervised learning uses labelled examples; the ‘unlabelled’ option describes unsupervised learning.

mcqs.q: You want a model to output every answer as a JSON object. Which approach most reliably gets the format right first time?
o: Ask once with no examples and hope
Put two or three worked input→output examples in the prompt (few-shot)
Repeat the word JSON many times
mcqs.e: Showing a few worked examples (few-shot prompting) demonstrates the exact format you want.

mcqs.q: Why do LLMs sometimes ‘hallucinate’ (state false things confidently)?
o: they optimise for plausible text, not verified truth
they are deliberately trying to deceive the user
they have simply run low on memory
they copy their answers directly from Wikipedia articles
mcqs.e: Models optimise for plausible-sounding text, not truth, so they can produce convincing errors.

mcqs.q: In “The cup fell off the table and it broke,” a transformer works out that “it” = the cup by…
o: using attention to weigh the other words
mcqs.e: Attention lets the model weigh which other words matter when resolving a word.

mcqs.q: An agent is asked for today's live exchange rate. At which step must it call a tool?
o: when it needs a fact it cannot know from training - to fetch the live rate
only at the very end, to format the text
mcqs.e: A tool call is needed exactly where the agent needs live/external information.

mcqs.q: Compared with writing a clever prompt, fine-tuning a model means…
o: training it further on extra examples
mcqs.e: Fine-tuning updates the model’s weights with new data; prompting only changes the input.

mcqs.q: An AI agent typically works in a loop of…
o: send request → wait → return one single reply
encode → store → then forget the result
compile → run → then exit the program
mcqs.e: Agents iterate: reason, take an action/tool call, read the result, and continue until the goal is met.

mcqs.q: A single neuron computes output = (w₁·x₁)+(w₂·x₂)+b. With x₁=2, x₂=3, w₁=1, w₂=2, b=−1, the output is…
mcqs.e: 2 + 6 − 1 = 7. This weighted sum + bias is the core operation inside every neural network.

mcqs.q: A realistic AI-generated video of a real person saying things they never said is a deepfake. A technical defence against this is…
mcqs.e: Provenance and watermarking help prove whether media is authentic or AI-generated.

mcqs.q: A model scores 99% on its training data but fails on new data. This is…
mcqs.e: Overfitting means the model memorised the training set instead of learning general patterns.

mcqs.q: An automatic moderation AI wrongly removes a harmless post (a false positive). The best response is to…
mcqs.e: Automated systems make mistakes; a human appeal route protects people from unfair errors.

mcqs.q: Most modern AI image generators are based on…
mcqs.e: Diffusion models start from random noise and denoise step by step into an image.

mcqs.q: Pasting a classmate’s private medical details into a public AI chatbot is risky mainly because…
o: it slightly slows down the assistant’s overall response time
it noticeably raises the compute cost
it can confuse the model’s text tokenizer
it can expose personal data that is stored or leaked
mcqs.e: Sharing others’ personal data (PII) can violate privacy and may be retained by the service.

mcqs.q: We test a model on data it never saw in training in order to…
o: make the whole training process run faster
shrink the final model’s size on disk
change the trained model’s output style
mcqs.e: A held-out test set measures real generalisation, not memorisation.

mcqs.q: The biggest societal risk of cheap, high-quality generative AI text is…
o: steadily rising electricity bills for everyday users
fewer available jobs for graphic designers
more crowded and noisy social media feeds
mcqs.e: Generative AI can mass-produce convincing misinformation, raising the need for verification and literacy.

mcqs.q: Build a tiny bigram predictor from this training text: “we play, we win, we play, we sing”. After the word “we”, which word should it predict?
mcqs.e: Count the pairs: “we”→play appears 2 times, “we”→win once and “we”→sing once. A bigram model predicts the most frequent next word - play (2 of 4). You just generated text the way a tiny language model does.

structured.title: Task 1 · Trace a Neuron and a Decision (First Principles)
structured.scenario:
A tiny model decides whether to recommend a video to a user. It is a single neuron:
z = (w₁·x₁) + (w₂·x₂) + b, then it applies a step activation: recommend if z > 0, else skip.
(A step activation is just an on/off switch. First work out the score z. If z is bigger than 0, the neuron switches ON → recommend. If not, it stays OFF → skip. Nothing in between.)

Features: x₁ = “matches user’s topic” (1 yes / 0 no), x₂ = “video length in minutes ÷ 10”.
Weights: w₁ = 4, w₂ = −1, bias b = 1.
parts: a) Compute z for Video P: x₁=1, x₂=2. Show working. Is it recommended?
b) Compute z for Video Q: x₁=0, x₂=0.5. Show working. Is it recommended?
c) In one or two sentences, explain what the negative weight w₂ tells us about how the model treats long videos.
d) Suggest one risk of recommending purely from such a score, and one improvement.

model.text: z = 4·1 + (−1)·2 + 1 = 4 − 2 + 1 = 3. 3 > 0 → Recommend. (4 for correct z, 2 for decision.)
model.rationale: Checks accurate step-by-step evaluation of a weighted sum plus a threshold activation.
Confirms the learner handles a 0 feature and decimals correctly.

model.text: A negative w₂ means longer videos lower the score, so the model is biased toward shorter videos.
model.rationale: Tests interpretation of weight sign - connecting maths to model behaviour.

model.text: Risk: it ignores quality/accuracy and can create filter bubbles or push only short content. Improvement: add more features, use human feedback, or include a diversity term.
model.rationale: Links a simple model to real recommender-system harms and mitigation - early systems thinking.

structured.totalNote: Full marks: correct z and decisions (a,b), correct interpretation of the negative weight (c), and a sensible risk + improvement (d).

structured.title: Task 2 · Program a Generative-AI Study Agent (Practical)
structured.scenario:
You will design an AI agent that helps a student revise. The agent can call these tools:
search(query) → returns notes · quiz(topic) → returns a practice question · ask_LLM(prompt) → returns generated text.
Write your answer as pseudocode (Python-like is fine).
parts: a) Write a function revise(topic) that: searches notes, asks the LLM to summarise them, then gives the student one quiz question. Use the tools above.
b) Add a loop so the agent keeps quizzing until the student answers 3 questions correctly. Track the count.
c) Dilemma: The student types “just tell me the exam answers.” Add a check in your code that refuses this and explains why, while still offering legitimate help. Briefly justify your design choice.

model.text:
e.g.
def revise(topic):
    notes = search(topic)
    summary = ask_LLM("Summarise: " + notes)
    print(summary)
    print(quiz(topic))
(Marks: calls search, ask_LLM, quiz in a sensible order with the topic passed through.)
model.rationale: Rewards correct tool use and data flow - the essence of an agent orchestrating tools.
Tests control flow and state - moving from a single call to an iterative agent loop.

model.text:
e.g.
if "exam answers" in request:
    return "I can’t give graded-test answers - that’s cheating. Want practice questions or an explanation instead?"
Justification: the agent should refuse harmful/unethical requests and redirect to legitimate help.
model.rationale: Embeds a guardrail in code and asks the student to justify it - practical ethics and the start of alignment thinking.

structured.totalNote: Full marks: working tool orchestration (a), a correct quiz loop with counter (b), and a coded refusal with justification (c).

structured.title: Task 3 · The Deepfake Dilemma (Theory + Ethics)
structured.scenario: A student newspaper receives a shocking AI-generated video appearing to show the school principal admitting to cheating in a competition. It could go viral before tomorrow’s big match. The editor must decide what to do tonight.
parts: a) Identify three things that could go wrong if the paper publishes the video without checking.
b) Describe two practical methods the team could use to check whether the video is real.

c) The student who supplied the video says, “Even if it’s fake, it makes people talk about cheating, which is a good cause.” Evaluate this argument - is a good cause a valid reason to publish a possible deepfake? Argue your position.
d) State one school-wide policy you would recommend for handling AI-generated media, with a reason.

model.text: Any three: defaming an innocent person; spreading misinformation; legal/disciplinary trouble; eroding trust in the paper; causing real harm before the truth emerges. (≈2 each, cap 5.)
model.rationale: Checks the student can foresee concrete harms of unverified generative media.

model.text: Any two: check provenance/metadata or watermarks; look for visual/audio artefacts; seek the original source; ask the principal directly; use a detection tool; corroborate with other evidence. (≈2–3 each.)
model.rationale: Rewards practical media-verification literacy rather than vague ‘ask someone’.

model.text: A strong answer argues that ends do not justify spreading falsehood: publishing a likely fake harms a real person, deceives readers, and damages credibility - the ‘good cause’ can be pursued honestly instead. Credit is given for a clear position supported by reasons; acknowledging the counter-view strengthens it.
model.rationale: This is the central dilemma. Marks reward reasoned ethical argument and engaging the opposing view, not a ‘correct’ slogan.

model.text: e.g., ‘verify-before-publish with a second source and a label for any AI-generated content,’ with a reason such as protecting people and reader trust.
model.rationale: Moves from judgement to governance - designing a rule that prevents the harm.

structured.totalNote: Full marks: foreseeable harms (a), real verification methods (b), a reasoned stance on the dilemma engaging the counter-argument (c), and a justified policy (d).
